extracted.intended_audience: general public and technology industry observers (startups, investors, policymakers) interested in software patents and patent litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating the quality, use, and monetization strategies of software patents — including how patents are prosecuted, bought, licensed, enforced by non-practicing entities, and how these practices affect startups and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / Prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must be new; many patents are 'essentially on things that have already been invented.' Experts found prior academic and business uses from the 1980s that undercut later software patents (e.g., David Martin and Rick McLeod's critiques of Crawford's patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess patent validity by searching historical prior art and contemporary implementations from the claimed priority date; if similar systems or methods were already in use, the patent likely should not have been issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and breadth of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents should not be so broad that they claim fundamental, widely-used behaviors; overly broad patents make 'everyone... guilty of infringement.' Crawford's patent appeared to cover many common Internet activities (upgrades, online purchases, cloud storage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claim breadth carefully — broad, vague claims that cover common practices are problematic and more likely to be accused of improper grant or to chill innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent corresponds to a real invention (substance over form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinction exists between a 'patent' and a genuine 'invention' — many software patents are seen by engineers as not reflecting actual inventive engineering (described by one engineer as 'mungo mumbo jumbo').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor patents tied to concrete technical contributions or implementations rather than abstract descriptions; examine technical substance, not just legalistic claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software patent eligibility and changing legal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically the patent office resisted software patents (viewed like language/copyright), but federal court decisions in the 1990s shifted this, triggering a 'flood of software patents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a software patent, consider the controlling judicial and PTO standards at the time of prosecution — changes in case law can affect whether a claim should have been allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercialization / practicing the patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents that lead to products or are practiced commercially are presented as more legitimate; Intellectual Ventures' lab produced few commercialized products while it amassed patents (most of IV's patents never made it into commercial use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the patent has been implemented or commercialized; absence of commercialization can be a signal the patent's value is primarily for assertion/monetization rather than tech progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality assessment via third-party review
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent assessment (e.g., M‑Cam) can reveal that many similar patents were issued around the same time, indicating questionable quality (example: thousands of contemporaneous patents with overlapping titles/content).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specialized prior-art and quality-analysis tools or firms to quantify redundancy, overlap, and the novelty of claims (e.g., counts of similar patents issued).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of patents as defensive insurance (mutually assured destruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large companies amass patent portfolios not to build products but to deter suits — 'mutually assured destruction' — purchasing patents to defend against litigation rather than to commercialize inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize portfolios held for defense change incentives in the market; evaluate patents in the context of strategic defensive posturing rather than technical merit alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and behavior of non-practicing entities (NPEs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some entities (NPEs / 'patent trolls') operate with no products or employees, set up shell companies in places like Marshall, Texas, and use acquired patents primarily to sue for licensing fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spot NPE patterns: empty offices, repeated suite addresses, no public operations; treat assertions from such entities with scrutiny regarding motive and ownership chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue selection and forum shopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs often file in courts perceived as favorable (e.g., Eastern District of Texas/Marshall), where cases may go to trial more quickly and juries may be more plaintiff-friendly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider forum-selection effects when assessing litigation risk and likelihood of enforcement success; venue can materially influence outcomes and settlement pressure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing practices and secrecy (NDAs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing arrangements with entities like Intellectual Ventures reportedly include extremely strict non-disclosure agreements; parties approached often avoid public comment out of fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that licensing terms and ownership arrangements may be secretive; inability to inspect licensing history and NDAs reduces market transparency and can indicate coercive monetization tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization structures and backend arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can be sold with backend royalty arrangements so sellers retain a share of downstream royalties; such arrangements can encourage aggressive enforcement by assignees (IV likely had 'back‑end arrangements' with Oasis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace assignment chains and financial arrangements (certifications of interested parties) to understand incentives that may drive litigation and licensing behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation economics and settlement incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants frequently settle because defending a suit can cost millions even when they might win at trial ('sometimes it makes more sense to settle and pay a license fee than to spend $2 million to $5 million on a court case').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in defense costs and settlement pressure when evaluating patent assertions; high litigation costs create a system where economic pressure can override merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents' impact on innovation and startups
rubrics_metrics.description: Many software engineers and investors believe the current patent climate hinders innovation, threatens startups, and raises the cost of bringing new products to market ('the average Silicon Valley start-up... aspects of what they're doing violate patents right now').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging patent policy or particular patents, consider their broader effects on innovation, entry barriers, and the competitive landscape — not only the rights of the patent holder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement-as-licensing paradigm
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation is characterized as 'just licensing by other means' — aggressive enforcement can be a primary monetization channel rather than cultivation of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret assertions and enforcement activity as part of a monetization strategy; evaluate whether enforcement supports genuine technology diffusion or functions purely to extract fees.
